issues.legal_issue: Property inherited by a male descendant under pre-statutory Mitakshara law from a paternal ancestor, and later allotted to his ancestor on partition, remains coparcenary property as to the male descendant.
material_facts: Succession to the property opened under the old Mitakshara law when the original owner died before the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 came into force.
The original owner’s son inherited the property, and the property was later partitioned among his sons.
The property allotted to the descendant’s father on partition was claimed by the descendant, who was born before his father’s purported sale of it.
issues.conclusion: The property allotted to the father remained coparcenary property as against his son, who acquired an interest in it by birth.
issues.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara law, property inherited by a male Hindu from a paternal ancestor within the relevant degrees is ancestral, and his male descendants acquire an interest in it by birth. Where succession opened before the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, that character is not altered by the Act’s later commencement. A share allotted on partition remains coparcenary property as regards the allottee’s male issue. The Court relied on Shyam Narayan Prasad v. Krisha Prasad, Yudhishter v. Ashok Kumar, and Valliammai Achi v. Nagappa Chettiar, as well as Mulla on Hindu Law; it distinguished Uttam v. Saubhag Singh because succession there opened after the Act came into force.

rule.if: ancestral_property_character_dispute and succession_opened_under_prior_mitakshara_law and inherited_from_paternal_ancestor and share_received_on_partition and male_descendant_claims_interest

predicates.ancestral_property_character_dispute: The case concerns whether inherited family property is coparcenary property as against a descendant.
predicates.succession_opened_under_prior_mitakshara: Succession to the property opened under the earlier Mitakshara law before the later statutory succession regime applied.
predicates.inherited_from_paternal_ancestor: A male ancestor inherited the property from a paternal ancestor.
predicates.share_received_on_partition: The ancestor later received the property or a share of it on partition.
predicates.male_descendant_claims_interest: A male descendant claims an interest in the property through that ancestor.

issues.definition: When the dispute concerns ancestral property inherited under the earlier Mitakshara law, later allotted on partition, and claimed by a male descendant, the property remains coparcenary as to that descendant.

issues.legal_issue: An alienation of coparcenary property is invalid when the alienee does not establish legal necessity, benefit to the estate, or adequate bona fide inquiry into either.
material_facts: The father sold property that remained coparcenary property as against his son.
The son had acquired an interest in the property by birth before the purported sale.
The purported buyer admitted that she paid no consideration, and the father also testified that no consideration was paid.
The buyer did not establish legal necessity, benefit to the estate, or bona fide inquiries into either.
issues.conclusion: The sale deeds were illegal, null and void, and were cancelled.
issues.legal_principle: A manager’s power to alienate coparcenary property is restricted to cases of legal necessity or benefit to the estate. The alienee bears the burden of establishing necessity or benefit, either by proving actual necessity or by showing proper and bona fide inquiries and reasonable steps to satisfy herself that necessity existed. The Court relied on Rani v. Santa Bala Debnath and Vijay A. Mittal v. Kulwant Rai, and on Mulla on Hindu Law.

rule.if: coparcenary_alienation_dispute and manager_alienated_joint_property and alienee_failed_to_prove_necessity_or_estate_benefit_or_bona_fide_inquiry and no_consideration_paid

predicates.coparcenary_alienation_dispute: The case concerns an alleged alienation of coparcenary property.
predicates.manager_alienated_joint_property: A person managing the coparcenary property purported to transfer it.
predicates.alienee_failed_to_prove_necessity_or_est: The transferee did not prove legal necessity, benefit to the estate, or reasonable bona fide inquiry into either.
predicates.no_consideration_paid: The purported transfer was made without payment of consideration.

issues.definition: When a manager purports to alienate coparcenary property without consideration and the transferee fails to establish necessity, estate benefit, or adequate inquiry, the alienation is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A transferee who acquired property from a transferor without valid title during pending litigation cannot obtain title through that transfer.
material_facts: A property suit challenging the original sale was pending when the purported buyer transferred the property to later purchasers.
The original sale was invalid, so the purported buyer had not acquired valid title to pass on.
issues.conclusion: The subsequent sale deed was null and void and was cancelled.
issues.legal_principle: Under the doctrine of lis pendens, a transfer made while litigation concerning the property is pending is subject to the outcome of that litigation; if the transferor is held to have no right or title, the transferee obtains no title. The Court relied on T.G. Ashok Kumar v. Govindammal.

predicates.property_title_suit_pending: A suit concerning rights or title to the property was pending.
predicates.transfer_occurred_during_litigation: The transferor purported to transfer the property while that suit was pending.
predicates.transferor_lacked_valid_title: The transferor did not have valid title to the property.

issues.definition: When property is transferred during a pending title suit by someone without valid title, the later transferee acquires no title.

issues.legal_issue: A coparcener whose interest is affected by an alleged unauthorized alienation has standing to seek a declaration that the alienation is invalid.
material_facts: The plaintiff was a male coparcener in the property by birth.
His father purported to sell the coparcenary property without establishing legal necessity or benefit to the estate.
The plaintiff sought a declaration that the sale deeds were invalid.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff had standing to bring the declaratory suit challenging the sale deeds.
issues.legal_principle: A coparcener whose interest in coparcenary property is directly affected by an alleged alienation may seek a declaration that the property could not be alienated without legal necessity or benefit to the estate; the plaintiff need not be an executant of the sale deed to challenge it on that basis.

predicates.declaratory_suit_challenging_coparcenary: The proceeding seeks a declaration that an alleged transfer of coparcenary property is invalid.
predicates.plaintiff_is_coparcener: The plaintiff holds an interest in the property as a coparcener.
predicates.alienation_affects_plaintiffs_interest: The alleged transfer affects the plaintiff’s interest in the property.

issues.definition: A coparcener has standing to seek a declaration against an alleged alienation when the suit challenges that alienation and it affects the coparcener’s interest.

issues.legal_issue: The non-production of land revenue records does not by itself defeat established title to property.
material_facts: The plaintiff did not produce certain land revenue records for earlier years.
The court concluded that the missing records did not affect title or ownership of the property.
issues.conclusion: The non-production of the land revenue records made no difference to the determination of title.
issues.legal_principle: The absence of land revenue records does not by itself determine or defeat ownership where it does not affect the title to the property.

predicates.property_title_dispute: The proceeding concerns ownership or title to property.
predicates.land_revenue_records_not_produced: A party did not produce relevant land revenue records.
predicates.missing_records_do_not_affect_title: The missing records do not alter or undermine the title evidence in the case.

issues.definition: In a property title dispute, missing land revenue records do not defeat title when their absence does not affect the title evidence.
